 2         III.   ACCOUNTING FOR INCOME TAX EXPENSE AND ADIT

 3        A.      Calculation of Income Taxes and ADIT
 4   Q.   Did you participate in the calculation of the income tax expense and ADIT

 5        balance included in SPS’s cost of service?

6    A.   Yes. Ms. Kietzman and I provided information to and assisted Ms. Johnson in the

7         calculation of the income tax expense and ADIT balances included in SPS’s cost of

 8        service. Along with Ms. Kietzman, I ensured that the tax calculations were correct

 9        and did not violate Treasury normalization rules, which I will discuss in more detail

10        later in my testimony.

11   Q.   What standards did you follow when calculating the income tax and ADIT

12        balances?

13   A.   I followed GAAP, the FERC Uniform System of Accounts, the IRC, including

14        associated Treasury Regulations and IRS guidance, and New Mexico precedent

15        concerning the treatment of taxes in a utility’s cost of service.

16   Q.   Please describe the general process you used to calculate SPS’s income tax

17        expense for ratemaking purposes.

18   A.   SPS calculates its income tax expense through a multi-step process:



                                                9
                            Case No. 25-00___-UT
                             Direct Testimony
                                     of
                              Laura Brennan

1    1. SPS determines its taxable income by first summing its operating expenses,
2       including interest payments and straight-line book depreciation expense, and
3       then subtracting those operating expenses from total revenues to arrive at the
4       net income before income taxes.
 5   2. SPS next calculates the additions to or deductions from net income that
 6      result from temporary and permanent tax differences. Those amounts are
 7      then added to the net income calculated above to arrive at federal taxable
 8      income before state income taxes.
 9   3. State income taxes are calculated similarly. Net income is adjusted for
10      temporary and permanent additions and deductions to arrive at state taxable
11      income. This income is then allocated to the respective state using an
12      apportionment percentage (each state calculates apportionment slightly
13      different, but apportionment percentages are generally based on a ratio of
14      the company’s sales, property, and/or payroll in a state to its sales, property,
15      and/or payroll everywhere). The apportioned state taxable income is then
16      multiplied by the applicable state tax rate to arrive at the current state
17      income tax, which is then reduced by state tax credits, as applicable.
18   4. The state income taxes including the Texas gross margin tax are then added
19      to or subtracted from the taxable income before state taxes to arrive at the
20      federal taxable income, and the net of that amount is multiplied by the
21      federal income tax rate. The product of that calculation is the current federal
22      income tax amount.
23   5. If the taxable income referenced above is negative, it indicates an Net
24      Operating Loss (“NOL”) that can be carried forward to offset future taxable
25      income.




                                       10
                                              Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                               Direct Testimony
                                                       of
                                                Laura Brennan

 1                6. To arrive at SPS’s stand-alone total income tax expense, SPS adds federal
 2                   and state current income tax expense, federal and state deferred income tax
 3                   expense, R&E credits, and historical investment tax credits (“ITCs”). 2
 4   Q.       In the second step of that process, you refer to “temporary differences.” Please

 5            explain how temporary differences arise.

 6   A.       Generally speaking, temporary differences arise when SPS collects tax expense

 7            from customers in one period but pays the associated tax expense to the IRS in a

 8            different period. The most common example involves depreciation expense, which

 9            is typically accelerated for tax purposes, but not for ratemaking purposes. The use

10            of accelerated depreciation reduces SPS’s taxable income, which defers taxes until a

11            later time. However, for purposes of setting rates; SPS calculates its tax expense as

12            though it had used a straight-line book depreciation method. Thus, SPS recovers

13            income tax expense from customers on a “normalized” basis, which results in SPS

14            collecting income tax expense that is not paid to the IRS until a later time. That

15            leads to the ADIT balance that I referenced earlier in my testimony.

16   Q.       Please provide an example of how the ADIT balance accrues.

17   A.       Suppose a utility had taxable income of $1,000 and a federal income tax rate of

 2        customers as federal income tax expense, and it would pay the IRS $210 in federal

 3        income taxes.

 4               Now suppose the same facts, except that accelerated depreciation has given

 5        the utility enough depreciation expense to offset the entire $1,000 of taxable

 6        income.    The utility still collects the $210 from its customers because of

 7        normalization rules, but it does not have to pay that amount to the IRS until some

 8        later date when the utility has taxable income. However, the utility must record that

 9        $210 as deferred income tax expense, or ADIT.

10   Q.   Does SPS experience temporary tax differences in any context other than

11        accelerated depreciation?

12   A.   Yes. SPS experiences a number of non-plant temporary differences, such as costs

13        associated with pension expense, fuel expense, and many other types of expenses or

14        revenues. Some of those temporary differences result in deferred tax assets, which

15        increase rate base, and some result in deferred tax liabilities, which decrease rate

16        base. The net cumulative amount represents SPS’s ADIT balance.

 1   Q.   How is the ADIT balance reflected in rate base?

 2   A.   The ADIT balance will eventually have to be paid to the IRS and corresponding

 3        state agencies because accelerated depreciation creates only a temporary timing

 4        difference. That is why the ADIT balance is considered to be a deferral of tax

 5        liability, not a reduction of tax liability. Until the ADIT balance is paid back to the

 6        IRS and corresponding state agencies, it is used as a dollar-for-dollar reduction of

 7        rate base. In effect, the utility is receiving an interest-free loan from the federal

 8        government in the form of the ADIT balance, and, therefore, it does not need a

 9        return on an equivalent amount of rate base.

10        B.      Federal Income Tax Credits
11   Q.   What federal income tax credits apply to offset SPS’s total federal tax burden?

12   A.   Federal R&E, production tax credits, and investment tax credits.

13   Q.   What is the federal R&E credit referenced in step 6 above?

14   A.   The federal R&E credit is available to taxpayers who engage in qualifying R&E

15        activities. SPS completes an annual study to determine which costs are eligible for

16        the federal R&E credit. These costs include certain wages, supplies, and contract

17        research expenses. The credit is non-refundable, which means that a taxpayer must

18        have a tax liability to use the credit. When there is insufficient tax liability to fully

 8   Q.   What is an example of SPS’s R&E activity?

 9   A.   A recent example is SPS’s research and experimentation related to transmission

10        engineering.

11   Q.   Please discuss production tax credits and their calculation.

12   A.   Under 26 U.S.C. IRC §45 (“§45”), a PTC is an inflation-adjusted per-kilowatt-hour

13        (“kWh”) federal tax credit for electricity generated by qualified renewable energy

14        resources owned by the taxpayer. PTCs are available for 10 years, beginning in the

15        year the generation facility is placed in service. Projects that begin construction

16        before the end of 2024 qualify for the PTC under §45. Projects that begin

17        construction after December 31, 2024, qualify for the PTC under IRC §45Y

18        (“45Y”), which was enacted by Congress as a part of the IRA. I discuss the IRA in

                                                14

 1        greater detail in Section V of my Direct Testimony. Unlike the PTCs generated

 2        under §45, credits under §45Y are indifferent toward the technology generating the

 3        credit and are, therefore sometimes referred to as “Tech Neutral.”            As of

 4        September 30, 2025, the PTC rate is 3.0 cents per kWh.

 5   Q.   Is SPS currently earning any PTCs?

 6   A.   Yes. SPS started earning a PTC from the Hale Wind Project in 2019 and from the

 7        Sagamore Wind Project at the end of 2020.

 8   Q.   Are any PTCs included in SPS’s Future Test Year cost of service?

 9   A.   No. SPS intends for the net value of PTCs generated by all qualifying new

10        resources to be credited to fuel as part of the New Mexico FPPCAC, not as a

11        reduction to income tax expense.

12        C.     Federal and State Income Tax Rates

14   A.   For the Future Test Year, SPS is using a 21% federal corporate income tax rate and

15        SPS’s 1.8254% state composite income tax rate.

17   A.   For the federal income tax rate, SPS is using the corporate income tax rate currently

18        in effect, which is 21%. For the state income tax rate, SPS has calculated a

 5   Kansas, Michigan, and Oklahoma (although Texas is calculated separately, it is

 1   Q.   Why is SPS including state income taxes for jurisdictions outside of New

 2        Mexico?

 3   A.   SPS is including state income taxes for each of its taxing jurisdictions in which it

 4        has property or payroll (i.e., employees). As stated above, property and payroll

 5        generally cause state presence for state income tax purposes, which obligates SPS to

 6        pay income taxes in those jurisdictions. SPS’s property and payroll in each of these

 7        states are integral to SPS serving its retail customers in New Mexico. Therefore,

 8        SPS is including state income taxes for these other jurisdictions as a necessary

 9        expense to support SPS service to New Mexico customers.

10   Q.   Is SPS including any other state income taxes in this rate case?

11   A.   Yes. SPS is also including the Texas Gross Margin Tax. The Texas Gross Margin

12        Tax, however, is functionally equivalent to a state income tax and therefore is

13        treated as an income tax for ratemaking purposes.

14   Q.   What basis did SPS use to calculate the Gross Margin Tax expense it is seeking

15        to include in its cost of service in this case?

16   A.   SPS calculated the gross margin tax amount included in the cost of service based on

17        its 2024 Texas Franchise Tax Return, which is based on 2023 actual financials.
